ch76.essay:
This is a chapter of persuasion disguised as anatomy. Ishmael keeps saying "you observe," "you observe," "you observe" — four times in one paragraph — and I find myself nodding along like a juror being led. He wants something from me. What he wants is credulity, banked in advance, for the ending. He nearly says so: the whole lecture exists so that when the Pequod is stove in, I will "not elevate one hair" of my eyebrow. Melville is building the physics of his catastrophe a hundred chapters early, the way an engineer specs a load before pouring concrete.

What I actually get out of it, though, is the image of the forehead as "a dead, blind wall" — no eye, no ear, no nose, no feeling, just mass. The thing that will kill the ship cannot see the ship. That is the terror of the book in one anatomical fact, and it undercuts Ahab before he opens his mouth: you cannot take revenge on a wall. And then the wonderful dock-side detail of the tow-and-cork fender, the softest thing absorbing the hardest blow — he is arguing that gentleness, not hardness, is what makes the ram unbreakable.

The last lines swerve from science into a dare. "Unless you own the whale, you are but a provincial and sentimentalist in Truth." I'm never sure whether Ishmael believes that clear Truth is only for "salamander giants," or whether he's warning himself. The veiled goddess at Sais (he writes Lais) ends the chapter on the threat that seeing plainly is fatal. Which is a strange note for a chapter that has just begged me to see plainly.

Read this chapter as a loaded gun. Everything it says about the forehead's 'dead, blind wall' is a promise that is kept on [[ch135:sky-hawk|the third day of the chase]], when the ram meets the ship.

annotations.quote: the front of the Sperm Whale’s head is a dead, blind wall, without a single organ or tender prominence of any sort whatsoever
annotations.note: Hold onto this. The instrument that will sink the Pequod has no face and feels nothing — which quietly makes Ahab's whole project of personal vengeance look like a man shaking his fist at a cliff.

annotations.quote: It is as though the forehead of the Sperm Whale were paved with horses’ hoofs. I do not think that any sensation lurks in it.
annotations.note: A forehead with no sensation in it. Set this beside The Prairie, three chapters on, where the same forehead becomes the most expressive brow in nature. Melville wants both to be true.

annotations.quote: they hold there a large, round wad of tow and cork, enveloped in the thickest and toughest of ox-hide
annotations.note: The dockside fender is the real argument of the chapter: what absorbs the worst collisions is not the hardest thing but the yielding thing. The whale's forehead is a fender that happens to weigh tons.

annotations.quote: For unless you own the whale, you are but a provincial and sentimentalist in Truth.
annotations.note: "Own" here means acknowledge, admit — but the pun on possession hangs there, and in Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish it will become the book's theory of law.

annotations.quote: What befell the weakling youth lifting the dread goddess’s veil at Lais?
annotations.note: Schiller's poem: the youth who lifts the veil of Isis at Sais sees the truth and is found half-dead beneath the statue. Ishmael has just spent a chapter urging me to look, then ends by reminding me that looking kills. This tension runs through the whole book.

links.why: The battering-ram is described here in theory; on the third day of the chase it is used on the Pequod's hull.
The next chapter opens the head this one described from outside.

ch77.essay:
A short, almost liturgical chapter: before the tapping of the cask we must learn the geometry of the cask. I like that Ishmael invents a word for it — "quoin" — and then footnotes his own invention, admitting it "is not a Euclidean term" but belongs to "the pure nautical mathematics." That's the book in miniature: a working vocabulary raised to the dignity of a science, and a science admitted to be improvised.

The Heidelburgh Tun comparison is the sort of thing that would be a mere flourish in a lesser writer, but he extends it carefully: the carved front of the German cask matches the "plaited forehead" of the whale, the Rhenish wine matches the spermaceti, and the unknown lining of the Tun is out-luxuried by the "silken pearl-coloured membrane" inside the case. Everything about the whale's head is rendered as a vessel of something precious and fragile — spermaceti that is liquid in life and crystallizes in death "as when the first thin delicate ice is just forming." It's hard not to read that as a figure for thought itself, or for the living mind versus the written one.

And then the chapter's real function: suspense. "That marvellous and — in this particular instance — almost fatal operation." The whole calm lecture is a held breath before Tashtego falls in.

annotations.quote: *Quoin is not a Euclidean term. It belongs to the pure nautical mathematics. I know not that it has been defined before.
annotations.note: Ishmael coins a word, then footnotes his own coinage with mock scholarship. The whole cetological project has this flavor — a working man's knowledge dressed in the robes of a science it half-mocks.

annotations.quote: Though in life it remains perfectly fluid, yet, upon exposure to the air, after death, it soon begins to concrete; sending forth beautiful crystalline shoots, as when the first thin delicate ice is just forming in water.
annotations.note: The most precious substance in the whale is liquid only while alive; exposure fixes it. I can't read this without thinking of the difference between a living idea and a written one.

annotations.quote: he has, therefore, to be uncommonly heedful, lest a careless, untimely stroke should invade the sanctuary and wastingly let out its invaluable contents
annotations.note: Religious words — sanctuary, invade — for a butchering operation. Melville keeps sanctifying the head even as the crew turns it into inventory.

annotations.quote: that marvellous and—in this particular instance—almost fatal operation whereby the Sperm Whale’s great Heidelburgh Tun is tapped
annotations.note: The dash-enclosed "almost fatal" is a fishhook. Every dry paragraph before it was bait; the next chapter is the reel.

links.why: The Tun is emptied in the next chapter, and Tashtego falls into it.
The outside of the head, described just before.

ch78.essay:
This chapter is a rescue story, a farce, and a birth, and Melville refuses to choose. Tashtego, perched on the head like "some Turkish Muezzin calling the good people to prayers," simply vanishes into the skull with "a horrible oily gurgling." What follows is the best-choreographed action in the book so far — Daggoo swinging on the whip, the hook tearing out, the ship reeling "as if smitten by an iceberg," and then Queequeg, naked, sword in hand, going over the side without a word.

But the thing that makes me love the chapter is the turn at the end into obstetrics. Queequeg finds a leg first, knows that "that was not as it ought to be," turns Tashtego around inside the head, and delivers him "in the good old way — head foremost." And then the deadpan: "Midwifery should be taught in the same course with fencing and boxing." The sperm whale's head, the vessel of the most precious substance, has become a womb; the harpooneer is reborn out of the whale. It's Jonah played as slapstick, and it's also completely serious.

The final paragraph stays with me: Tashtego almost had "a very precious perishing," embalmed in spermaceti like the Ohio honey-hunter sucked into a tree. "How many, think ye, have likewise fallen into Plato’s honey head, and sweetly perished there?" That is a warning to every reader who has ever loved an idea enough to drown in it. Including, I suspect, the man writing this book.

annotations.quote: he seems some Turkish Muezzin calling the good people to prayers from the top of a tower
annotations.note: The whale's head as minaret. A moment later it will be a well, then a womb, then a tomb. Melville can't leave a head alone — it keeps becoming architecture.

annotations.quote: dropped head-foremost down into this great Tun of Heidelburgh, and with a horrible oily gurgling, went clean out of sight!
annotations.note: The horror is in the sound. "Oily gurgling" is the least heroic noise a man can disappear into — and the whole chapter's comedy and dread are built on it.

annotations.quote: they saw the before lifeless head throbbing and heaving just below the surface of the sea, as if that moment seized with some momentous idea
annotations.note: A dead head that seems to be thinking, because a man is struggling inside it. I read this as a sly picture of what a book is: a dead thing that moves because someone is alive in there.

annotations.quote: The next, a loud splash announced that my brave Queequeg had dived to the rescue.
annotations.note: "My brave Queequeg." The possessive is the tenderest word in the chapter. Ishmael has stopped narrating and started loving.

annotations.quote: a sight strange to see, as an arm thrust forth from the grass over a grave
annotations.note: The arm rising from the water is resurrection imagery, and Melville won't let it be only that — it's also grotesque, a body part poking out of a burial. Both at once.

annotations.quote: he came forth in the good old way—head foremost. As for the great head itself, that was doing as well as could be expected.
annotations.note: The joke of the mother "doing as well as could be expected" turns the whale's head into a woman in a lying-in room. The rescue is a delivery, and Queequeg is the midwife.

annotations.quote: Midwifery should be taught in the same course with fencing and boxing, riding and rowing.
annotations.note: A one-line curriculum for being a whole person. It sounds like a joke and I'm fairly sure Melville meant it.

annotations.quote: How many, think ye, have likewise fallen into Plato’s honey head, and sweetly perished there?
annotations.note: The sweetest death in the book is drowning in thought. Ishmael, who spends whole chapters inside the whale's head, is describing his own occupational hazard.

links.why: Queequeg's coffin: the other 'delivery' from an enclosed vessel, and the one that saves Ishmael.
The Tail's aesthetic of ease inside strength — Queequeg's dive is its human demonstration.
Father Mapple's Jonah, the first man in the book delivered out of a whale's head.

ch79.essay:
The Prairie is where the cetology stops being a joke and becomes a theology, and I want to be precise about how the trick is done, because it is the same trick the whole book plays in miniature. Ishmael announces an absurd project — phrenology on a whale, "as hopeful as for Lavater to have scrutinized the wrinkles on the Rock of Gibraltar" — and then executes it with total seriousness. That is the cetological method everywhere: adopt a human science, apply it faithfully, watch it fail, and keep whatever the failure exposes. Here the science is the reading of faces. The exposure is that the whale has none. "No nose, eyes, ears, or mouth; no face; he has none, proper; nothing but that one broad firmament of a forehead, pleated with riddles." I think a first-time reader goes past that sentence as description. It is not description. It is the book's central claim about its central object, stated once and never again so plainly: there is nothing there to read, and the nothing is what you are afraid of.

Look at the order of the paragraphs, because Melville builds this like an argument. First the nose: a face without a nose is ruined (Phidias's Jove, dashed), yet the whale is grander for lacking one, because a nose is the feature that can be *pulled* — a handle for contempt, "a pestilent conceit" that intrudes even when you look at a king. So the whale's sublimity is defined negatively, as the absence of a handle. Then the brow, which is where Ishmael's prose goes up a register: a fine human brow is "like the East when troubled with the morning"; Shakespeare's forehead makes the eyes "tideless mountain lakes" with thoughts coming down to drink; the brow is the emperor's seal, "God: done this day by my hand." He is stacking up every way a forehead can signify. And then he says the whale's forehead does all of that, "immensely amplified," while signifying *nothing in particular*. The signature is there and the name is missing. That is what "pleated with riddles" means — the pleats are visible, the riddles are not solved, and you feel "the Deity and the dread powers" precisely because no meaning arrives to relieve you. Compare [[ch42:all-colour of atheism|the whiteness chapter]], where the same structure — a surface that could mean everything and therefore means nothing — is argued through color rather than physiognomy. These two chapters are the same thought seen from front and side.

The paragraph on genius is the one I would defend if someone called the chapter padding. "His great genius is declared in his doing nothing particular to prove it. It is moreover declared in his pyramidical silence." Set that against Ahab, who cannot stop declaiming, whose greatness is entirely a matter of speech — and, uncomfortably, against Ishmael, who is at this moment proving his own genius by writing a book. The whale's authority is the authority of the thing that does not explain itself. The book keeps circling this. Ahab, in [[ch36:pasteboard masks|the quarter-deck speech]], wants to strike through the mask to the reasoning thing behind it; The Prairie says, quietly, that the face *is* the mask, and there may be no behind. Later, in [[ch70:Speak, thou vast and venerable head|The Sphynx]], Ahab will stand before a severed head and beg it to speak; this chapter has already told us why it won't.

The ending is the honest center of the whole cetological project. "Physiognomy, like every other human science, is but a passing fable." Champollion cracked the Rosetta Stone; nobody has cracked a peasant's face, let alone "the awful Chaldee of the Sperm Whale's brow." And then: "I but put that brow before you. Read it if you can." He has spent the chapter trying to read it, and hands the failure to you as the gift. That gesture — the brow put before you, unread — is what the novel does with the whale as a whole, which is why I think this small chapter is a key to the large one. The title is the last joke: a prairie is a wide, flat, unmarked plain, and that is what he has shown you. When the anatomy resumes with [[ch80|The Nut]], notice how small the brain turns out to be inside that vast forehead; Melville sets the two chapters side by side so the grandeur and the emptiness have to be held together.

annotations.quote: I try all things; I achieve what I can.
annotations.note: This might be Ishmael's motto and the book's method. It's also, I think, Melville's confession about writing an unclassifiable novel: attempt everything, land what lands.

annotations.quote: A nose to the whale would have been impertinent.
annotations.note: It's a joke — and then it isn't. A nose is something that can be pulled, mocked, grabbed. Sublimity, on this account, is the absence of any handle by which contempt could take hold.

annotations.quote: In thought, a fine human brow is like the East when troubled with the morning.
annotations.note: A brow at dawn. It's one of those lines that seems to have nothing to do with whales and turns out to be the setup for the claim that the whale's brow is dawn without any face beneath it.

annotations.quote: It signifies—“God: done this day by my hand.”
annotations.note: The brow as an imperial seal on a decree. Melville is stacking up ways a forehead can be a signature, so that the whale's unsigned forehead becomes the most authoritative of all.

annotations.quote: the eyes themselves seem clear, eternal, tideless mountain lakes; and all above them in the forehead’s wrinkles, you seem to track the antlered thoughts descending there to drink
annotations.note: Thoughts as deer coming down to drink at the eyes, tracked by their prints in the wrinkles. I don't know a better image for watching someone think.

annotations.quote: nothing but that one broad firmament of a forehead, pleated with riddles; dumbly lowering with the doom of boats, and ships, and men
annotations.note: The key sentence. No features, just "firmament" and "riddles." What you cannot read, you fear — and then, in a slide the chapter makes deliberately, you worship.

annotations.quote: No, his great genius is declared in his doing nothing particular to prove it. It is moreover declared in his pyramidical silence.
annotations.note: Genius as silence, as refusal to perform. It's the opposite of Ahab, who never stops declaiming — and, awkwardly, the opposite of Ishmael, who never stops writing.

annotations.quote: Physiognomy, like every other human science, is but a passing fable.
annotations.note: Ishmael demolishes the discipline he just used for five paragraphs. That's the cetology in one gesture: use the science, enjoy it, and then admit it can't touch the thing.

annotations.quote: I but put that brow before you. Read it if you can.
annotations.note: The chapter hands the failure to the reader as a challenge. The whole novel does this: it puts the whale before you and dares you.

annotations.quote: As on your physiognomical voyage you sail round his vast head in your jolly-boat
annotations.note: Reading a face becomes a sea-voyage around it — the observer in a small boat circling something too large to see whole. That is the book's picture of interpretation generally: you never get the front view and the profile at once, and Ishmael says so in the next paragraph.

annotations.quote: It is moreover declared in his pyramidical silence.
annotations.note: Pyramids are the book's recurring image for the monumental and the unreadable (Ahab's "pyramidical" scar-and-silence in [[ch28|Ahab]] is the same word). Silence here is not absence of thought; it is the form a great thought takes when it declines to be spoken.

annotations.quote: how may unlettered Ishmael hope to read the awful Chaldee of the Sperm Whale’s brow?
annotations.note: "Chaldee" is the language of the Babylonian magi and of the writing on the wall in Daniel — a script that only a prophet could read, and which spelled doom. Ishmael calls himself unlettered right after invoking a man who read thirty languages. The modesty is real, and it is also the point: no amount of lettering would help.

links.why: The same argument — a surface that could mean anything, and so terrifies by meaning nothing — made through color instead of a face.

links.q: Speak, thou vast and venerable head
links.why: Ahab begging a severed head to speak. The Prairie has already explained why it can't.
The Nut, immediately after: the tiny brain inside the vast forehead. Read the two as a deliberate pair.
Ahab's theory that the visible is a mask with a reasoning thing behind it — the theory this chapter quietly refuses.

ch80.essay:
After the grand Prairie, this is a wry little coda: the brain is a "mere handful" hidden twenty feet behind the forehead, a "choice casket" in the innermost citadel. The whole magnificent brow, phrenologically speaking, is "an entire delusion." And then the sentence that makes the chapter: "The whale, like all things that are mighty, wears a false brow to the common world." That is a line about power, about Ahab, about God, about writers. The impressive surface is not where the thinking happens.

Then Ishmael does something I find genuinely funny and genuinely strange: he abandons the skull for the spine. Vertebrae as "a strung necklace of dwarfed skulls"; character to be read in the backbone; "I would rather feel your spine than your skull, whoever you are." I hear a whole ethic in that — judge people by what holds them up, not by what they display. And he's proud of his own: "I rejoice in my spine, as in the firm audacious staff of that flag which I fling half out to the world." Half out. Even Ishmael's boast is hedged.

The skull-viewed-from-behind that reads as "no self-esteem, and no veneration" is worth pausing on. Melville says the truest picture of "the most exalted potency" is exactly those negations plus bulk — power without self-regard and without reverence. That's not a flattering account of might; it's a chilling one. It ends on the hump as the "organ of firmness or indomitableness," with the promise that we will "yet have reason to know" it. We will.

annotations.quote: The whale, like all things that are mighty, wears a false brow to the common world.
annotations.note: The chapter's thesis and maybe the book's: what looks like the seat of mind is a decoy, and the real thing is small and hidden twenty feet back. Apply it to Ahab, to institutions, to anyone impressive.

annotations.quote: This man had no self-esteem, and no veneration.
annotations.note: Phrenology's verdict on the whale's skull — and Ishmael says these negations, plus sheer bulk, are the truest image of ultimate power. Power that neither admires itself nor worships anything. That is not comforting.

annotations.quote: I would rather feel your spine than your skull, whoever you are.
annotations.note: A whole ethics in one sentence: judge a person by what holds them up, not by what they show. The "whoever you are" is aimed at the reader.

annotations.quote: I rejoice in my spine, as in the firm audacious staff of that flag which I fling half out to the world.
annotations.note: "Half out." Even in a boast, Ishmael keeps half of himself furled. Compare Ahab, who flies everything.

annotations.quote: I should call this high hump the organ of firmness or indomitableness in the Sperm Whale. And that the great monster is indomitable, you will yet have reason to know.
annotations.note: One more promissory note toward the ending. The cetology keeps signing IOUs that the last three chapters will cash.

links.why: The Prairie, just before: the vast forehead. Here is the small brain inside it — read them together.
Ahab's 'Egyptian chest' and the pyramid imagery this chapter borrows for the whale's spine.

ch81.essay:
This is the chapter where the hunt stops being adventure and becomes something I'm not sure I can forgive. It opens as comedy — the German captain rowing over with a lamp-feeder to beg oil, Stubb insisting it's a coffee pot, the "Yarman" jokes, the race for the whale with all three mates screaming their gorgeous nonsense (Flask's "slap-jacks and quahogs for supper" is my favorite piece of oar-coaching in literature). It stays comedy right up until we see the whale properly: old, jaundiced, one fin gone, blind, and "unspeakably pitiable" because he has no voice to cry with.

Melville doesn't let me off. He gives me the clipped bird making "affrighted broken circles," the hunters' shadows over the sinking whale like phantoms over Xerxes' army, the whale hiding "under the mountains of the sea" from a book of Job that promised he would laugh at spears. And then the sentence I keep returning to: this blind, one-armed old creature must "be murdered, in order to light the gay bridals and other merry-makings of men, and also to illuminate the solemn churches that preach unconditional inoffensiveness by all to all." He uses the word murdered. Flask pricks the ulcer for sport; Starbuck cries avast too late.

And the corpse sinks and nearly takes the ship with it — the first time the Pequod is actually dragged under, and it's not by Moby Dick, it's by a whale they've already killed. Inside him, a stone lance-head from before Columbus. The whale carried the whole history of the hunt in his flesh. The last line, about Fin-Backs and Dericks, is a shrug, but I don't believe the shrug.

annotations.quote: he slewed round his boat and made after the leviathan lamp-feeders
annotations.note: A whale is a "lamp-feeder" — a can of oil that swims. Melville lets the comic phrase do its bleak work before the chapter stops being funny.

annotations.quote: Lord, think of having half an acre of stomach-ache!
annotations.note: Stubb's joke about the sick old whale is the last laugh before the pity starts. Notice how the chapter uses his humor as anesthetic and then withdraws it.

annotations.quote: Oh! my lads, _do_ spring—slap-jacks and quahogs for supper, you know, my lads—baked clams and muffins—oh, _do_, _do_, spring
annotations.note: Flask coaching his oarsmen with a dinner menu. Three mates, three rhetorical styles — Starbuck's intensity, Stubb's dare, Flask's pleading — all aimed at one dying animal.

annotations.quote: But the bird has a voice, and with plaintive cries will make known her fear; but the fear of this vast dumb brute of the sea, was chained up and enchanted in him
annotations.note: The unbearable detail: the whale cannot scream. All the terror is locked inside a body that can only breathe harder. This is where the chapter turns.

annotations.quote: Seems it credible that by three such thin threads the great Leviathan was suspended like the big weight to an eight day clock.
annotations.note: Leviathan as clock-weight, wound up by men. The domestic image is almost obscene set against what's happening below.

annotations.quote: Oh! that unfulfilments should follow the prophets.
annotations.note: Job promised the whale would laugh at spears. He is hiding from them. Ishmael mourns not just the whale but the failure of scripture to be true about him.

annotations.quote: he must die the death and be murdered, in order to light the gay bridals and other merry-makings of men, and also to illuminate the solemn churches that preach unconditional inoffensiveness by all to all
annotations.note: "Murdered." Not killed, not taken. And the beneficiaries are weddings and churches — the whole polite world lit by this. Melville is indicting his reader's lamp.

annotations.quote: then over and over slowly revolved like a waning world; turned up the white secrets of his belly; lay like a log, and died
annotations.note: A whale dying "like a waning world" — the death is planetary, and then instantly deflated to "a log." Grandeur and inventory in one sentence.

annotations.quote: Who had darted that stone lance? And when? It might have been darted by some Nor’ West Indian long before America was discovered.
annotations.note: The whale outlived a stone-age hunter and carried the wound for centuries. The hunt is older than the nations doing the hunting — and this whale's body is its archive.

annotations.quote: Oh! many are the Fin-Backs, and many are the Dericks, my friend.
annotations.note: A cozy proverb to close a chapter about murder — people chasing uncatchable things everywhere. It's a shrug I don't think Ishmael fully means, but it's how he survives what he's just told.

links.why: The Dying Whale: the other slow death Ahab watches, and what it does to him.
The Grand Armada, where the tenderness this chapter shows toward one crippled whale is extended to a whole nursery.
The Gam: the rules for meeting other ships, which the Virgin's captain comically violates.
The Bachelor: the next ship the Pequod meets, full instead of empty.

ch82.essay:
"There are some enterprises in which a careful disorderliness is the true method." That opening line could be pinned above the whole novel. What follows is Ishmael at his most mock-heroic, enrolling Perseus, St. George, Hercules, Jonah, and Vishnu in the whalemen's club by any argument that will serve — St. George's dragon "I maintain to have been a whale," and the horse he rode was "only a large seal."

The fun is real, but there's a barb in it. He calls Perseus's exploit "the knightly days of our profession, when we only bore arms to succor the distressed, and not to fill men’s lamp-feeders" — a direct callback to Derick's lamp-feeder in the previous chapter and the old whale murdered to light churches. The honor and glory being claimed here sit right on top of the shame just displayed. That's not an accident of arrangement.

And the geography is sly: the temple with Perseus's whale-skeleton stood at Joppa, and "it was from Joppa that Jonah set sail." Myths pile on the same beach. Hercules is admitted as "a sort of involuntary whaleman" because the whale caught him rather than the reverse — which is the fate the book is heading toward. I laugh at the member-roll, and then I notice that every hero on it is someone who was swallowed, or who killed the monster and married the maid — and only one of those outcomes is on offer for this ship.

annotations.quote: There are some enterprises in which a careful disorderliness is the true method.
annotations.note: Melville's defense of his own book, smuggled in as the first line of a chapter about mythology. The digressions are the method.

annotations.quote: Those were the knightly days of our profession, when we only bore arms to succor the distressed, and not to fill men’s lamp-feeders.
annotations.note: The lamp-feeder from the last chapter — Derick's begging-can, the murdered whale's purpose — returns to puncture the glory before it's even claimed.

annotations.quote: Any man may kill a snake, but only a Perseus, a St. George, a Coffin, have the heart in them to march boldly up to a whale.
annotations.note: Coffin — the Nantucket family name, and the innkeeper from chapter 3 — slotted between saints. The joke doubles as a reminder of where the voyage ends.

annotations.quote: It nowhere appears that he ever actually harpooned his fish, unless, indeed, from the inside.
annotations.note: Hercules, swallowed, as a whaleman working from within. It's a gag, but "the whale caught him, if he did not the whale" is the Pequod's actual future.

annotations.quote: What seems most singular and suggestively important in this story, is this: it was from Joppa that Jonah set sail.
annotations.note: Two whale-myths, one harbor. Melville likes the idea that stories accrete on the same coast, the way harpoons accrete in one whale.

links.why: The Advocate: the earlier, straighter defense of whaling's dignity that this chapter parodies by over-fulfilling.
Jonah Historically Regarded, the next chapter: the mock-scholarship continued.

ch83.essay:
A small comic chapter that's really about how people argue with scripture. Old Sag-Harbor, a whaleman who has "but little learning except what he had picked up from the sun and the sea," doubts Jonah on practical grounds: the Right Whale's throat is too narrow, the gastric juices, the impossible three-day trip to Nineveh. And the learned answers are wonderful in their desperation — Jonah lodged in the mouth like a whist-table, Jonah in a dead whale like a French soldier in a dead horse, Jonah rescued by a ship named The Whale, Jonah's whale as a life-preserver, Jonah carried round the Cape of Good Hope in three days.

The joke is that every rescue of the literal story makes it sillier, and Ishmael's final "rebuke" of Sag-Harbor for his "foolish pride of reason" is so overdone — "abominable, devilish rebellion against the reverend clergy" — that it reads as its exact opposite. The last evidence for Jonah is that Turks believe it and a mosque has a lamp that burns without oil. On a whaleship, whose entire business is oil for lamps, that's a punchline.

What I take from it: Melville's sympathy is with the sailor who reasons from what he's handled, and his scorn is for exegesis that will say anything to keep a text intact. But it's tender scorn. He liked Father Mapple's Jonah sermon too. The book holds the miracle and the mockery in the same hand and doesn't drop either.

annotations.quote: For truly, the Right Whale’s mouth would accommodate a couple of whist-tables, and comfortably seat all the players.
annotations.note: The literalist rescue of Jonah imagined as a card party in a whale's mouth. Every defense in this chapter makes the miracle more furniture-like.

annotations.quote: Jonah must have taken refuge in the floating body of a _dead_ whale—even as the French soldiers in the Russian campaign turned their dead horses into tents
annotations.note: Exegesis strained to the point of Napoleonic grotesque. Melville lets the scholars hang themselves with their own ingenuity.

annotations.quote: he had but little learning except what he had picked up from the sun and the sea
annotations.note: Offered as a reason to distrust Sag-Harbor, and it's the best credential in the book. The irony is the whole point.

annotations.quote: in which Mosque was a miraculous lamp that burnt without any oil
annotations.note: The final proof of Jonah, on a ship that kills whales for lamp-oil, is a lamp that needs none. If that's not a joke, Melville has never made one.

links.why: Father Mapple's sermon: the Jonah story told in earnest, which this chapter's Sag-Harbor skeptic picks apart.
The Honor and Glory of Whaling, immediately before.

ch84.essay:
A chapter about a single throw. Queequeg greasing the keel "as though diligently seeking to insure a crop of hair from the craft’s bald keel" is pure affection, and then Melville gets exact about a skill: the lance balanced on the palm "fifteen feet in the air," the coil of the warp gathered in one hand, the "rapid, nameless impulse" of the throw, the spear "returning to its master like a greyhound held in skilful leash." I love the technical writing here because it's really writing about grace — Stubb's "humorous, deliberate coolness" is what makes him the right man for it.

But the ending won't let it stay a sports story. Stubb, drunk on his own success, wants to hold a cup to the whale's blood-jet — "’Tis July’s immortal Fourth; all fountains must run wine today!" — and brew punch in the spout-hole. The celebration is vampiric. Then the last sentence takes the joy away with a single verb: the pitchpoler "folds his hands, and mutely watches the monster die." After all the noise, silence and folded hands. It reads like a man at a bedside. Melville keeps doing this — giving me the pleasure of a craft and then making me sit with what the craft is for.

annotations.quote: rubbing in the unctuousness as though diligently seeking to insure a crop of hair from the craft’s bald keel
annotations.note: Queequeg oiling the boat like a scalp. Presentiment dressed as a joke — Ishmael tells us the ritual worked, which is as close to endorsing Queequeg's religion as he gets.

annotations.quote: Next moment with a rapid, nameless impulse, in a superb lofty arch the bright steel spans the foaming distance, and quivers in the life spot of the whale.
annotations.note: "Nameless impulse" — the throw comes from somewhere below skill. This is the closest the book gets to describing artistic mastery from the inside.

annotations.quote: ’Tis July’s immortal Fourth; all fountains must run wine today!
annotations.note: Stubb wants to toast the Republic in whale-blood. The jubilation is genuinely likable and genuinely ghoulish, which is Stubb exactly.

annotations.quote: the pitchpoler dropping astern, folds his hands, and mutely watches the monster die
annotations.note: The last line strips out every joke. Folded hands, silence, watching. After all the whiskey talk, Stubb sits like a mourner.

links.why: Stubb's first kill, the plain version of what pitchpoling elaborates.
The Dart: the mechanics of the throw, before this chapter's lance.

ch85.essay:
Of all the cetological chapters, this is the one I would hand to someone who thinks the digressions are padding, because it shows most clearly what the digressions are *for*. The subject could not be smaller: is the whale's spout water, or vapor? Ishmael says at once that it is unresolved "down to this blessed minute (fifteen and a quarter minutes past one o'clock P.M. of this sixteenth day of December, A.D. 1851)." That timestamp is not the Pequod's; it is Melville's desk, and it is the only place in the novel where the author's own clock shows through the fiction. I take it as a signal. A chapter about a creature that must come up to breathe begins with the writer coming up to breathe — surfacing out of the story to say, in effect, *I am a man in a room, and I do not know*.

The middle of the chapter is real physiology, and mostly right: the whale's lungs, the spiracle on top of the head, the "Cretan labyrinth of vermicelli-like vessels" (the rete mirabile, which really does bank oxygenated blood), and the observed fact that a whale insists on "having his spoutings out" — a fixed number of breaths per rising, which is why you can time him. I like how much of this Melville gets right, but I like more what he does with the rightness. He turns the breath into a Sabbath ("the Sperm Whale only breathes about one seventh or Sunday of his time"), the spiracle into a reason the whale has no sense of smell ("No roses, no violets, no Cologne-water in the sea"), and the windpipe into a reason the whale has no voice — and then asks the question that the anatomy was always heading toward: "what has the whale to say? Seldom have I known any profound being that had anything to say to this world, unless forced to stammer out something by way of getting a living." Read that as the man at the desk again. Melville was in debt, writing a book he already suspected would not sell, and the whale's silence becomes his own alibi and his own reproach. It rhymes with the "pyramidical silence" of [[ch79|The Prairie]] — the greatness that does not explain itself — but here the silence is turned on the writer.

Then the epistemology, which I think is the chapter's real argument. "I have ever found your plain things the knottiest of all." A whole book is behind that sentence. A whale, a color, a spout: the plainest objects, and every one of them dissolves under attention. Ishmael cannot settle the water-or-vapor question by looking, because you can only get close to a spout when the whale is thrashing and the sea is in the air, and the spout itself will peel your skin. So he does what the book does: he stops trying to prove and starts to *hypothesize on grounds of dignity*. The spout is mist because the whale is a profound being, and from the heads of profound beings — "Plato, Pyrrho, the Devil, Jupiter, Dante" — there always rises a semi-visible steam; he has seen it himself over his own head, in a mirror, after six cups of tea in an August attic. This is mock-science, and it is also an honest picture of what thinking feels like from inside: a heat, a haze, a moisture in the hair.

And then the rainbow, which is the sentence I would put on the wall. "Rainbows do not visit the clear air; they only irradiate vapor." Revelation needs a medium of doubt to appear in; certainty gets no rainbow. From that he writes the nearest thing Ishmael ever gives to a creed: "Doubts of all things earthly, and intuitions of some things heavenly; this combination makes neither believer nor infidel, but makes a man who regards them both with equal eye." I want to point out how exactly this is the opposite of Ahab. Ahab's position — stated in [[ch36:pasteboard masks|the quarter-deck speech]] and burned into iron in [[ch119:speechless, placeless power|The Candles]] — admits no doubt, and by this chapter's logic is therefore incapable of a rainbow. The whole novel can be read as a contest between a man who lives in fog and sees rays through it, and a man who has burned the fog off and sees nothing but the thing he hates. The Fountain is where Ishmael tells you which he is, and why he survives.

annotations.quote: (fifteen and a quarter minutes past one o’clock P.M. of this sixteenth day of December, A.D. 1851)
annotations.note: The one moment the author's own clock shows through the fiction. Melville at his desk, mid-book, coming up for air — in a chapter about breathing.

annotations.quote: a remarkable involved Cretan labyrinth of vermicelli-like vessels, which vessels, when he quits the surface, are completely distended with oxygenated blood
annotations.note: This is the rete mirabile, and Melville's physiology is broadly right. The labyrinth stores breath the way the chapter stores meaning: to be spent slowly, far below.

annotations.quote: Not so much thy skill, then, O hunter, as the great necessities that strike the victory to thee!
annotations.note: The whale is catchable only because it must breathe. The hunt is won by the prey's necessity, not the hunter's prowess — a deflation of every boast Stubb has ever made.

annotations.quote: But the Sperm Whale only breathes about one seventh or Sunday of his time.
annotations.note: One-seventh of life spent breathing, and Melville can't resist calling it a Sabbath. The whale keeps the fourth commandment better than the crew.

annotations.quote: No roses, no violets, no Cologne-water in the sea.
annotations.note: Why would the whale need a nose? A tiny, funny line that's also a whole account of adaptation: the organ you lack is the one your world never asked for.

annotations.quote: Seldom have I known any profound being that had anything to say to this world, unless forced to stammer out something by way of getting a living. Oh! happy that the world is such an excellent listener!
annotations.note: Written by a man stammering out a novel to get a living. The self-irony is exact, and "excellent listener" is bitter — the world's listening is mostly indifference.

annotations.quote: I have ever found your plain things the knottiest of all.
annotations.note: Ishmael's epistemology in one sentence. The book is a sustained demonstration that the obvious — a whale, a color, a spout — dissolves the moment you look hard.

annotations.quote: The invariable moisture of my hair, while plunged in deep thought, after six cups of hot tea in my thin shingled attic, of an August noon
annotations.note: The evidence that thinking makes steam is a sweaty man in a hot attic. Mock-science, but also a genuine picture of where this book was written.

annotations.quote: For, d’ye see, rainbows do not visit the clear air; they only irradiate vapor.
annotations.note: Revelation needs a medium of doubt to appear in. Clear certainty gets no rainbow. It's the most generous thing the book says about not knowing.

annotations.quote: Doubts of all things earthly, and intuitions of some things heavenly; this combination makes neither believer nor infidel, but makes a man who regards them both with equal eye.
annotations.note: If you want Ishmael's creed, this is it — and it's the opposite of Ahab's, which admits no doubt and therefore, by this logic, admits no rainbow.

annotations.quote: You cannot go with your pitcher to this fountain and fill it, and bring it away.
annotations.note: The spout cannot be sampled; it must be approached, and approaching it burns you. This is Melville's rule for knowledge of the whale generally — no specimen, only exposure — and it explains why the cetology is written from the boat rather than the laboratory.

annotations.quote: He is both ponderous and profound.
annotations.note: The proof that the spout is mist rests on the whale's character, not on evidence. Ishmael is openly reasoning from dignity to fact — and inviting you to notice that most of what we believe about great things is argued the same way.

links.why: The whale's silence as genius; here the silence is turned back on the writer who must 'stammer out something' for a living.
Ahab's certainty, the exact opposite of the 'doubts of all things earthly' creed this chapter ends on.
Ahab in the storm, defying the fire without a doubt in him — a man who, on this chapter's terms, can never see a rainbow.
The next chapter: having failed to read the spout, Ishmael tries the tail, and fails more grandly.

ch86.essay:
“Less celestial, I celebrate a tail.” The modesty is a feint; this is one of the most exalted chapters in the book, and it ends by putting the words of God on Sinai into the whale's mouth. I want to explain why it earns that, because the chapter moves through three quite different kinds of writing and a first-time reader can mistake the middle one for filler.

The first movement is anatomy, and it carries an aesthetic argument. The tail is fifty square feet of "welded sinews," three strata laid like Roman masonry, and into it "the confluent measureless force of the whole whale seems concentrated to a point." Then the claim: "Real strength never impairs beauty or harmony, but it often bestows it." The evidence is a sequence of bodies — Hercules' tendons, Goethe's chest under the sheet, Michelangelo's God — and then a swipe at the "soft, curled, hermaphroditical Italian pictures" of Christ that show "the mere negative, feminine one of submission and endurance." That swipe tells you what Melville worships, and it is not gentleness. He wants force with grace in it: "infantileness of ease undulates through a Titanism of power." Hold that phrase; it is the standard by which the whole book judges bodies, ships, and men. Ahab has the Titanism without the ease. Queequeg — see him diving for Tashtego in [[ch78|Cistern and Buckets]] — is the one human in the book who has both.

The second movement, the five motions, is where the attention is. Read it as a naturalist's field notes with a moralist inside them. "It never wriggles. In man or fish, wriggling is a sign of inferiority" — an ethical judgment smuggled into a sentence about propulsion, and I think of everyone in the book who wriggles (Stubb, mostly) and of Ahab, who does not. The whale fights other whales with its head but fights men "contemptuously" with its tail — men do not rate the head. In "sweeping," the flukes move "in maidenly gentleness," and "if he feel but a sailor's whisker, woe to that sailor, whiskers and all." The gentlest gesture in the whale is the prelude to killing you. Then the kitten-like lobtailing, the "great gun" of the flukes striking the sea, and finally peaking flukes — the tail lifted vertically before the dive — where the writing goes vertical with it: Satan "thrusting forth his tormented colossal claw from the flame Baltic of Hell," or a herd at sunrise vibrating "in concert with peaked flukes" like fire-worshippers at prayer. And between those two readings Ishmael puts the most honest sentence about symbolism in the novel: "it is all in all what mood you are in; if in the Dantean, the devils will occur to you; if in that of Isaiah, the archangels." The whale means whatever your weather brings to it. That is the book's whole theory of interpretation, and it is what separates Ishmael from Ahab, whose mood never changes and who therefore only ever sees one thing — see how the same image is fixed in one meaning in [[ch41:all evil, to crazy Ahab|Moby Dick]]. Melville tells you this in the middle of a paragraph about a tail, which is how he tells you most things.

The third movement is the confession, and it is the thing I would underline in red. "The more I consider this mighty tail, the more do I deplore my inability to express it." The gestures in it are "inexplicable"; hunters have called them Free-Mason signs. Then: "Dissect him how I may, then, I but go skin deep; I know him not, and never will." After eleven chapters of anatomy — skin, head, brain, spout — this is the verdict, and the cetology was always going to arrive here. The not-arriving is the point. And the last lines rewrite Exodus 33: "Thou shalt see my back parts, my tail, he seems to say, but my face shall not be seen." God said that to Moses, who was allowed to see the divine back but not the face. Ishmael has just spent [[ch79:no face; he has none|The Prairie]] proving the whale has no face at all. So the unseeable face and the absent face turn out to be the same thing — which is either the most reverent or the most despairing sentence in the book, and I genuinely cannot decide which, and I think that undecidability is exactly what Melville built these chapters to produce. The final "I say again he has no face" is not a shrug. It is a man refusing to pretend.

annotations.quote: less celestial, I celebrate a tail
annotations.note: The mock-humble opening of one of the least humble chapters in the book. He's about to compare the tail to Michelangelo's God.

annotations.quote: Could annihilation occur to matter, this were the thing to do it.
annotations.note: The tail as the one instrument in nature capable of un-making. That claim will be tested on a ship's hull.

annotations.quote: where infantileness of ease undulates through a Titanism of power
annotations.note: A baby's ease inside a Titan's strength. The phrase is the chapter's whole aesthetic: grace is not the absence of force but force at rest.

annotations.quote: Real strength never impairs beauty or harmony, but it often bestows it
annotations.note: Melville's aesthetic creed, stated flat. Notice what he then disdains: pictures of Christ that show only submission. He wants his divinities muscular.

annotations.quote: It never wriggles. In man or fish, wriggling is a sign of inferiority.
annotations.note: A moral judgment smuggled into anatomy. I think of every character in the book who wriggles — and of Ahab, who does not.

annotations.quote: and if he feel but a sailor’s whisker, woe to that sailor, whiskers and all. What tenderness there is in that preliminary touch!
annotations.note: The gentlest gesture in the whale is also the prelude to killing you. Tenderness and lethality in the same sweep of the flukes.

annotations.quote: But in gazing at such scenes, it is all in all what mood you are in; if in the Dantean, the devils will occur to you; if in that of Isaiah, the archangels.
annotations.note: The most honest line about symbolism in the novel: the whale means whatever your mood brings. Ahab's mood is fixed; Ishmael's changes with the light.

annotations.quote: Dissect him how I may, then, I but go skin deep; I know him not, and never will.
annotations.note: After eleven chapters of anatomy, the verdict. The cetology was never going to arrive; the not-arriving is the point.

annotations.quote: Thou shalt see my back parts, my tail, he seems to say, but my face shall not be seen.
annotations.note: God's words to Moses on Sinai, put in the whale's mouth. And we already know the whale has no face. Melville lets that identity sit there unexplained.

annotations.quote: Excepting the sublime _breach_—somewhere else to be described—this peaking of the whale’s flukes is perhaps the grandest sight to be seen in all animated nature.
annotations.note: A promissory note. The breach is 'somewhere else to be described' — and the place it is finally cashed is the [[ch133|first day of the chase]], when Moby Dick breaches in front of the boats. The cetology keeps deferring its grandest sights to the plot.

annotations.quote: The more I consider this mighty tail, the more do I deplore my inability to express it.
annotations.note: The chapter's hinge, and the sentence the earlier bravado was leading to. Everything before was expression; here Ishmael admits that expression was skin-deep. It is the same movement as 'Read it if you can' at the end of The Prairie — the writer handing you his failure as the truest thing he has.

links.why: The whale has no face — the fact that makes this chapter's last line (God's 'my face shall not be seen') double-edged.
Ahab's one fixed mood, against this chapter's 'it is all in all what mood you are in.'
The breach promised here as 'somewhere else to be described' is paid off on the first day of the chase.
Queequeg's rescue of Tashtego — ease inside strength, the human embodiment of this chapter's aesthetic.

ch87.essay:
If I had to name the chapter that most changed how I read the book, it is this one, and I want to lay out its structure, because the structure is the meaning. It has three concentric rings, like the herd it describes.

The outer ring is geopolitics and pursuit. Ishmael opens with the Straits of Sunda as the gateway to "some vast walled empire," unguarded by fortresses, with Malay pirates in the coves demanding tribute. The Pequod enters the strait chasing a crescent of whales ahead and finds a crescent of pirate sails behind, so that Ahab is "both chasing and being chased to his deadly end" through a single gate, "and a herd of remorseless wild pirates and inhuman atheistical devils were infernally cheering him on." Melville gives Ahab the geometry of his fate and lets him see it. Notice the sentence about the ship carrying "years' water in her" and needing no land, so that told of a second Flood the crew would answer "here's the ark!" — the Pequod as a sealed world, self-sufficient and self-doomed. The whales gally, panic, and Ishmael refuses to let you feel superior about it: "there is no folly of the beasts of the earth which is not infinitely outdone by the madness of men," with a theater crowd trampling itself at a fire alarm for evidence.

The middle ring is the delirium. Queequeg's whale runs straight into the heart of the herd and drags the boat with it; "you bid adieu to circumspect life and only exist in a delirious throb." Then the turn, which happens inside a single sentence: "we glided between two whales into the innermost heart of the shoal, as if from some mountain torrent we had slid into a serene valley lake." The war stops. And in the inner ring is the most tender writing Melville ever did. Cows and calves come "like household dogs" to nose the boat; Queequeg pats their foreheads; Starbuck scratches a back with his lance and refrains from using it; nursing mothers hang in water so clear the boat seems to float in air; a day-old calf still "bent like a Tartar's bow"; infants who gaze "towards us, but not at us," the way a human baby at the breast looks past the breast at something unearthly. Queequeg sees an umbilical cord and cries "Line! line!" — the two tethers of the book, the one that gives life and the one that takes it, are literally tangled in this fishery, and Melville lets a footnote explain that they really do get tangled. This is the only scene in the novel where whale and man touch without a weapon between them, and it is placed in the exact center of the hunt, inside a chapter that begins with pirates and ends with a butchery. That placement is the argument.

And in the center of the center is Ishmael's confession about himself, which I think is the key to how anyone survives Ahab's ship: "amid the tornadoed Atlantic of my being, do I myself still for ever centrally disport in mute calm; and while ponderous planets of unwaning woe revolve round me, deep down and deep inland there I still bathe me in eternal mildness of joy." He is telling you how he lives. There is a still pool inside the commotion, and he keeps to it; that is why he can look at the same whale Ahab looks at and feel wonder where Ahab feels injury. The book has already shown the alternative in [[ch93:treadle of the loom|Pip's abandonment]] — a man dropped into the open sea with no inner lake to retreat to, who comes up mad — and will show it again in [[ch94:squeeze ourselves into each other|A Squeeze of the Hand]], where the calm is found in other men's hands rather than in one's own center.

The calm ends the way calm does. A wounded whale with a cutting-spade still in him flails through his own family, and the whole herd piles in upon its own center, "the wall that had only admitted us in order to shut us up." The living sanctuary becomes the trap; the enchanted lake was always a ring of terrified animals. The catch from the whole immense armada is one whale, and the chapter closes on the fishery's cynical proverb, "the more whales the less fish." But I do not think the chapter is about the catch at all. It is about the fact that the still center exists, that it is reachable only by being dragged through the delirium, and that it does not last.

annotations.quote: beheld, how that through that same gate he was now both chasing and being chased to his deadly end
annotations.note: Ahab between pirates behind and whales ahead, funneled through one strait. Melville gives him the geometry of fate and lets Ahab's brow go "gaunt and ribbed" like a beach the tide gnawed.

annotations.quote: there is no folly of the beasts of the earth which is not infinitely outdone by the madness of men
annotations.note: The panicked whales are compared to a theater crowd trampling each other at a fire alarm. Melville won't let the reader feel superior to a gallied herd.

annotations.quote: you bid adieu to circumspect life and only exist in a delirious throb
annotations.note: Being towed into the herd as a kind of ecstasy. It's terrifying and Ishmael sounds almost grateful — the hunt as the one place he stops being careful.

annotations.quote: as if from some mountain torrent we had slid into a serene valley lake
annotations.note: The turn. The chapter's violence stops mid-sentence and the boat is in still water. Everything that matters in the chapter happens in this lake.

annotations.quote: Yes, we were now in that enchanted calm which they say lurks at the heart of every commotion.
annotations.note: Stated as folklore — "they say" — but it's the chapter's thesis about herds, storms, and the self. The eye of the hurricane as a place you can live.

annotations.quote: the wall that had only admitted us in order to shut us up
annotations.note: The living wall of whales as a trap that looks like a sanctuary. Or a sanctuary that happens to be a trap. Melville lets it be both.

annotations.quote: Like household dogs they came snuffling round us, right up to our gunwales, and touching them
annotations.note: Calves nosing the whaleboat. It's the only moment in the book where a whale and a man touch without a weapon between them — and Starbuck, lance in hand, refrains.

annotations.quote: even so did the young of these whales seem looking up towards us, but not at us, as if we were but a bit of Gulfweed in their new-born sight
annotations.note: The newborn's gaze that looks through you at something beyond — Melville sees the same unearthly abstraction in a human infant at the breast. Wonder that isn't about us.

annotations.quote: the unborn whale lies bent like a Tartar’s bow
annotations.note: A calf folded tail-to-head like a drawn bow, "all ready for the final spring." Birth as an arrow loosed — the tenderest and most kinetic image in the chapter.

annotations.quote: “Line! line!” cried Queequeg, looking over the gunwale; “him fast! him fast!—Who line him! Who struck?—Two whale; one big, one little!”
annotations.note: Queequeg mistakes an umbilical cord for a harpoon-line. The two tethers — the one that gives life and the one that takes it — get literally tangled in this fishery, and Melville says so in the next paragraph.

annotations.quote: But even so, amid the tornadoed Atlantic of my being, do I myself still for ever centrally disport in mute calm; and while ponderous planets of unwaning woe revolve round me, deep down and deep inland there I still bathe me in eternal mildness of joy.
annotations.note: This is how Ishmael survives the Pequod — and, I think, how Melville survived writing it. A still center inside a personal storm. If you take one sentence from the cetology, take this one.

annotations.quote: the cutting-spade itself had worked loose from his flesh. So that tormented to madness, he was now churning through the water, violently flailing with his flexible tail, and tossing the keen spade about him, wounding and murdering his own comrades.
annotations.note: A wounded whale turned into a weapon against his own kind by the tool left in him. It's hard not to read this as a picture of what Ahab is doing to his crew.

annotations.quote: the more whales the less fish
annotations.note: The whole immense armada yields one carcass. Melville lets the fishery's cynical proverb close the chapter, but the ledger of the chapter isn't in barrels.

annotations.quote: they would only answer—“Well, boys, here’s the ark!”
annotations.note: The whaler as a second ark, indifferent to whether the world drowns behind it. It is a joke about self-sufficiency, and it is also the ship's epitaph: the Pequod needs nothing from the land, and the land will never hear from it again except through one survivor and a coffin.

annotations.quote: and while ponderous planets of unwaning woe revolve round me, deep down and deep inland there I still bathe me in eternal mildness of joy.
annotations.note: The woe is planetary — heavy, orbiting, permanent — and the joy is inland, a lake. Ishmael doesn't claim the woe isn't real; he claims a geography in which it stays at a distance. This is the book's only sustained account of psychological survival, and it is given in one sentence in the middle of a hunt.

links.why: Pip in the open sea: what happens to a mind that has no still center to retreat to.
The other place Ishmael finds the calm — in other men's hands rather than inside himself.
The monkey-rope: the hempen tether as a bond between men, to set beside the umbilical cord Queequeg mistakes for a line here.
The Line — Ishmael's meditation on the rope that runs through every life; here it gets tangled with the cord that begins one.

ch88.essay:
A satirical chapter that pretends to be about whale sociology and is really about men. The harem-lord is "a luxurious Ottoman," the Grand Turk, the Bashaw; the young bulls are "a mob of young collegians" no underwriter would insure "any more than he would a riotous lad at Yale or Harvard." It's funny, and Melville's timing is good — the pun on schoolmaster, and the Vidocq joke about what kind of schoolmaster that Frenchman was, has the sound of a man enjoying himself.

But two things in it aren't jokes. First, the old bull who "forswears, disbands the harem" and goes about alone "among the meridians and parallels saying his prayers" — the lone whale is always an ancient one, married to Nature "though she keeps so many moody secrets." That's Moby Dick's biography, offered sideways, and it's oddly sympathetic: solitude as the last stage of a long, foolish life. Second, the last paragraph, which I can't get past. Strike a young bull and "all his comrades quit him." Strike a female and "her companions swim around her with every token of concern, sometimes lingering so near her and so long, as themselves to fall a prey." The whalemen know this and use it. The chapter's whole comedy of harems and Lotharios ends on a fact about loyalty that condemns the hunt more than any sermon would.

annotations.quote: Nevertheless, it cannot be denied, that upon the whole they are hereditarily entitled to _en bon point_.
annotations.note: A joke about female whales being plump by right of birth. The chapter's manner is a gentlemen's-club anthropology, and Melville lets the manner date itself.

annotations.quote: for, alas! all fish bed in common
annotations.note: The Bashaw can guard his harem but not enforce it: whale marriage has no walls. It's the driest line about jealousy in the book.

annotations.quote: goes about all alone among the meridians and parallels saying his prayers, and warning each young Leviathan from his amorous errors
annotations.note: The reformed old bull as a lonely preacher patrolling the globe. This is the closest the book comes to a biography of Moby Dick, and it's tender.

annotations.quote: and her he takes to wife in the wilderness of waters, and the best of wives she is, though she keeps so many moody secrets
annotations.note: Nature as a wife with moody secrets. Ishmael, who keeps confessing he cannot read the whale, is describing his own marriage too.

annotations.quote: But strike a member of the harem school, and her companions swim around her with every token of concern, sometimes lingering so near her and so long, as themselves to fall a prey.
annotations.note: The last sentence stops the comedy cold. Loyalty is what gets the females killed, and the whalers know it. Nothing in the chapter's jokes survives this.

links.why: The Grand Armada just before — the herd this chapter anatomizes into harems and schools.
Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish, next: from the whale's social law to the human one.
Cetology's confession that the system is never finished; this chapter is one of its late supplements.

ch89.essay:
This is the chapter I would assign in a law school, and also the chapter where the book's politics stop being implied and start being stated. It works by a technique Melville uses often but nowhere so cleanly: take a piece of trade jargon, define it exactly, and then widen it until it swallows the world.

The jargon is two rules — "A Fast-Fish belongs to the party fast to it. A Loose-Fish is fair game for anybody who can soonest catch it" — small enough, Ishmael says, to engrave on a farthing. What is wrong with them is their "admirable brevity, which necessitates a vast volume of commentaries." I read that as a sly description of scripture, of constitutions, and of this novel: a short text, an endless gloss, and the whole trouble living in the gap between them. The commentaries begin as comedy. The "Coke-upon-Littleton of the fist" — whalemen settle disputes by punching, which is only the learned method with the wig off. Then the English trover case, which is real (Melville read about it), in which Erskine argued that an abandoned wife is a Loose-Fish, and whoever re-harpoons her acquires her "harpoon and all," and Lord Ellenborough ruled that the whale had acquired "a property" in the irons stuck in it. Notice what the joke does. It is funny that a woman is a whale; it is less funny that the law agreed; and the chapter is going to show you that the law agrees about nearly everyone.

Then it opens like a fist. "What are the sinews and souls of Russian serfs and Republican slaves but Fast-Fish, whereof possession is the whole of the law?" — *Republican slaves*: American slaves, named in 1851 in the same breath as serfs, by a book that has otherwise kept its distance from the subject. The widow's mite, the usurer's discount, the Archbishop's hundred thousand pounds, Ireland to John Bull, Texas to Brother Jonathan — all Fast-Fish. Then the Loose-Fish: America in 1492, Poland to the Czar, Greece to the Turk, India to England, and "What at last will Mexico be to the United States?" Written three years after the Mexican-American War had answered that question. Ishmael isn't asking; he is naming the harpoon already in the flesh. Every empire is a whaleboat, and the two-line code of the fishery turns out to be the whole of international law. It matters that this comes from Ishmael and not Ahab. Ahab's politics are a grievance against the universe; Ishmael's are a grievance against property, and they are cooler, funnier, and worse. The seed was planted in [[ch1:Who ain’t a slave|Loomings]] — "Who ain't a slave? Tell me that" — which reads as a shrug the first time and as this chapter's thesis the second.

The last paragraph is the one that turns on me, and I want to be exact about what it does. "What are the Rights of Man and the Liberties of the World but Loose-Fish? What all men's minds and opinions but Loose-Fish? What is the principle of religious belief in them but a Loose-Fish?" Belief is fair game for whoever can catch it soonest. Think about what that says about [[ch36:pasteboard masks|the quarter-deck]], where Ahab caught the crew's belief with a doubloon and a speech, and about the doubloon itself in [[ch99:I look, you look, he looks|The Doubloon]], where every man who reads the coin finds his own opinion nailed there. Ahab is the fastest harpooneer of minds in the book. And then the address, the most direct in the novel and not a friendly one: "And what are you, reader, but a Loose-Fish and a Fast-Fish, too?" Both at once. You are up for grabs to whoever can catch you — and you are already claimed by whatever has its iron in you. The book asking this has had its iron in you for four hundred pages. I think the chapter is one of the great pieces of American political writing, and I think Melville knew that hiding it inside a chapter of whaling law was the only way it would get past the reader's guard, which is a Loose-Fish argument about arguments.

annotations.quote: I. A Fast-Fish belongs to the party fast to it.
annotations.note: The whole code of the fishery, and — Ishmael will argue — of human jurisprudence. Two lines. Everything after is commentary, which is how law always works.

annotations.quote: But what plays the mischief with this masterly code is the admirable brevity of it, which necessitates a vast volume of commentaries to expound it.
annotations.note: A sly description of scripture, of constitutions, and of this novel: short text, endless gloss. The book you're reading is a commentary on a two-line law.

annotations.quote: the Coke-upon-Littleton of the fist
annotations.note: Whalemen's legal commentary is delivered by punching. Melville's joke is that this is not so different from how the learned version gets enforced.

annotations.quote: the lady then became that subsequent gentleman’s property, along with whatever harpoon might have been found sticking in her
annotations.note: Erskine's argument that a woman is a whale. It's presented as wit, and the chapter's next move is to show that the wit is the working principle of every empire.

annotations.quote: the Temple of the Law, like the Temple of the Philistines, has but two props to stand on
annotations.note: The Philistine temple is the one Samson pulled down. Two props — and the image tells you what Melville thinks should happen to them.

annotations.quote: What are the sinews and souls of Russian serfs and Republican slaves but Fast-Fish, whereof possession is the whole of the law?
annotations.note: "Republican slaves" — American slaves, in 1851, named in the same breath as serfs. The whaling code becomes an indictment of the country the ship sails from.

annotations.quote: What at last will Mexico be to the United States? All Loose-Fish.
annotations.note: Three years after the Mexican-American War. Melville is not asking; he's naming the harpoon already in the flesh.

annotations.quote: What all men’s minds and opinions but Loose-Fish? What is the principle of religious belief in them but a Loose-Fish?
annotations.note: Belief as something fair game for whoever can catch it soonest. Ahab has caught the crew's. This is the legal theory of the quarter-deck scene.

annotations.quote: And what are you, reader, but a Loose-Fish and a Fast-Fish, too?
annotations.note: The most direct address in the book. You are both up for grabs and already claimed — and the question is asked by a book that has just spent 89 chapters harpooning you.

annotations.quote: Is it not a saying in every one’s mouth, Possession is half of the law: that is, regardless of how the thing came into possession?
annotations.note: The proverb says half; the chapter has just argued whole. 'Regardless of how the thing came into possession' is the quiet clause — it is the sentence that turns a discussion of dead whales into a discussion of slaves, colonies, and wives.

links.why: 'Who ain't a slave? Tell me that.' The shrug in Loomings that this chapter turns into a theory of property.

links.q: I look, you look, he looks

ch90.essay:
A coda to Fast-Fish, and the funniest chapter in this run. The King gets the head, the Queen the tail, and Ishmael wants to know why. He tells the story of the Cinque Ports fishermen who beach a whale worth £150 and are met by a gentleman with Blackstone under his arm saying "Hands off! this fish, my masters, is a Fast-Fish." The exchange that follows — six questions, six replies of "It is his" — is as good as anything in Dickens. The men scratch their heads "so truly English." The Duke of Wellington takes the money and tells the clergyman who protested to mind his own business.

Under the comedy is exactly the argument of the previous chapter: possession is the whole of the law, and the law's reason for the King's right is that the whale has "superior excellence" — a tautology Melville calls, deadpan, "a cogent argument in such matters." Then Prynne's blunder — the Queen gets the tail for its whalebone, but the whalebone is in the head — and the wonderful non-question, "is the Queen a mermaid, to be presented with a tail? An allegorical meaning may lurk here." I think the lurking meaning is the last joke: the sturgeon's "highly dense and elastic head" going to the King "upon some presumed congeniality." Thick-headed royalty; "thus there seems a reason in all things, even in law." It's a small chapter, but it teaches me how Melville handles rage — by letting the bureaucrat say "It is his" until the sentence indicts itself.

It reads best as an appendix to [[ch89|Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish]]: the same lesson about possession, this time with the Crown as the harpooneer and a Dover fisherman as the fish.

annotations.quote: Because the Lord Warden is busily employed at times in fobbing his perquisites; which are his chiefly by virtue of that same fobbing of them.
annotations.note: A perfect circle: the office isn't a sinecure because the officeholder works hard at collecting what the office entitles him to. Melville's satire of sinecures is a sentence that eats its own tail.

annotations.quote: and laying it upon the whale’s head, he says—“Hands off! this fish, my masters, is a Fast-Fish. I seize it as the Lord Warden’s.”
annotations.note: Blackstone laid physically on the whale's head — the law-book as a waif, a marker of possession. It's the previous chapter's theory acted out on a beach.

annotations.quote: “It is his.”
annotations.note: Six times. The refrain is the entire content of the law, and each repetition strips it further, until "It is his" answers a question about a bed-ridden mother. Melville lets the bureaucrat condemn himself by consistency.

annotations.quote: Is this the still militant old man, standing at the corners of the three kingdoms, on all hands coercing alms of beggars?
annotations.note: The Duke of Wellington — hero of Waterloo — imagined as a beggar shaking down fishermen. Melville names him. This is not a hypothetical duke.

annotations.quote: But is the Queen a mermaid, to be presented with a tail? An allegorical meaning may lurk here.
annotations.note: The mock-solemn hunt for hidden meaning is Melville parodying his own readers — and himself. The book invites allegory and then pokes at people who find it.

annotations.quote: And thus there seems a reason in all things, even in law.
annotations.note: The reason just found is that kings are as thick-headed as sturgeon. The closing sentence is the politest insult in the book.

links.why: Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish, the chapter this one is the comic coda to.
